records.title: Philosophical Foundations of the American Revolution
records.heading: Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence
records.text:
Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence
Common Sense and the Declaration turned republican and natural-rights ideas into a public case for independence that Americans would cite for generations.
The belief in republican government found expression in Thomas Paine's Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence. Paine's pamphlet, published in January 1776, attacked monarchy and hereditary rule, argued that it was absurd for a continent to be governed by an island, and called for independence in plain language that ordinary readers could follow. It was widely read and helped turn colonial opinion away from reconciliation with Britain.
The Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776. Thomas Jefferson was the principal author. The Declaration stated that all men are created equal and have unalienable rights, that governments derive their powers from the consent of the governed, and that people may change or abolish a government that violates those rights. It then listed grievances against King George III.
The ideas in these documents resonated throughout American history, shaping Americans' understanding of the ideals on which the nation was based. Later reformers appealed to the Declaration's language of equality and rights to demand that the nation live up to its principles.

records.title: The American Revolution
records.text:
The American Revolution
How the war began, the turning points that saved the Patriot cause, and why Britain's apparent advantages were not enough to defeat the colonies.
Despite loyalist opposition and Britain's apparent military and financial advantages, the Patriot cause succeeded because of the combined effects of the colonists' own efforts and help from abroad.
The CED asks you to explain how various factors contributed to the American victory. Be ready to rank the factors and to say why a single cause is not enough.

records.title: The American Revolution
records.heading: The war begins
records.text:
The war begins
The war began in Massachusetts in 1775, widened into a fight for independence by 1776, and divided colonists into Patriots and Loyalists.
Fighting began in April 1775 when British troops marching to seize colonial military supplies clashed with militia at Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts. The Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia, created the Continental Army, and named George Washington its commander. In July 1775 Congress sent the Olive Branch Petition to the king, who rejected it, and in July 1776 Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence.
Not all colonists supported the Patriot cause. Loyalists, who stayed faithful to the Crown, were a substantial minority, and some regions, especially in the South and in parts of New York, were bitterly divided. The war was in part a civil war among colonists.

records.title: The American Revolution
records.heading: Turning points
records.text:
Turning points
Saratoga brought the French alliance, and the allied victory at Yorktown led to the Treaty of Paris of 1783.
After early defeats in 1776, Washington's surprise victory at Trenton at the end of the year lifted Patriot morale. The Patriot victory at Saratoga in New York in 1777 convinced France that the Americans could win. In 1778 France signed an alliance with the United States, and soon provided money, supplies, troops, and naval power. Spain and the Netherlands later joined the war against Britain, which turned the conflict into a wider European and global war.
The Continental Army endured the hard winter at Valley Forge in 1777–1778 and emerged better trained. After 1778 the British shifted their effort to the South, but they struggled to hold territory there. In 1781, a combined American and French army and French fleet trapped a British army under General Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, and he surrendered in October. The Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized American independence and set the new nation's boundaries from the Atlantic to the Mississippi River.

records.title: The American Revolution
records.heading: Why the Patriots won
records.text:
Why the Patriots won
Colonial effort, leadership, commitment, and European help together overcame Britain's advantages.
The Patriot cause succeeded because of the actions of colonial militias and the Continental Army, George Washington's military leadership, the colonists' ideological commitment and resilience, and assistance sent by European allies. Washington kept the army together through defeat and hardship and avoided the destruction of his forces. Militias controlled their local areas and wore down British forces. Many Patriots remained committed to republican ideals even when the war went badly.
Britain faced its own problems. Its armies were thousands of miles from home, the colonies were too large to occupy, and British leaders could not win the support of enough colonists to hold the territory that their soldiers captured. French assistance, in money, equipment, soldiers, and sea power, was decisive at Yorktown.
Do not credit one cause alone. The French alliance mattered, but it came after Saratoga showed that the Patriots could fight, and it did not remove the need for Washington's army or local militias.

records.title: The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
records.text:
The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
How Revolutionary ideals of equality and liberty led some Americans to challenge slavery and expand political participation, how women's roles were redefined, and how the Revolution inspired movements abroad.
The Revolution's ideals made inequalities in American society harder to ignore, but they were applied unevenly and left slavery and many exclusions in place.
The CED asks you to explain the various ways the Revolution affected society and to describe its global impact. Look for both the change that Revolutionary ideals produced and the limits on that change.
records.excerpt: How Revolutionary ideals of equality and liberty led some Americans to challenge slavery and expand political participation, how women's roles were redefined, and how the Revolution inspired movements abroad.

records.title: The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
records.heading: Equality, slavery, and political democracy
records.text:
Equality, slavery, and political democracy
The Revolution encouraged antislavery action and wider political participation, but both advanced unevenly.
During and after the American Revolution, an increased awareness of inequalities in society motivated some individuals and groups to call for the abolition of slavery and greater political democracy in the new state and national governments. Many Patriots saw a contradiction between demanding liberty from Britain and holding people in slavery. Quakers and other reformers led antislavery efforts, and enslaved and free Black Americans petitioned for freedom, used the courts, and some served in the Continental Army.
The result was uneven. Vermont's 1777 constitution banned slavery, Pennsylvania began gradual emancipation in 1780, and Massachusetts courts ended slavery in the state in the 1780s, while other northern states adopted gradual emancipation laws in the years that followed. Slavery remained central to the economy of the South. In 1775 Virginia's royal governor, Lord Dunmore, offered freedom to enslaved people who left rebel owners and joined the British, and thousands of enslaved people fled to British lines during the war.
Calls for greater political democracy also appeared in the new state governments. Some states widened participation, but property qualifications for voting remained common, and women and most free Black men could not vote in most states.

records.title: The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
records.heading: Women and republican motherhood
records.text:
Women and republican motherhood
Republican motherhood gave women a civic role as teachers of republican values, without political equality.
Women contributed to the Revolutionary cause by boycotting British goods, running farms and businesses, raising money, nursing the wounded, and following the army. In response to women's participation in the American Revolution, Enlightenment ideas, and women's appeals for expanded roles, an ideal of “republican motherhood” gained popularity. It called on women to teach republican values within the family and granted women a new importance in American political culture.
Abigail Adams, writing to her husband John Adams while he served in Congress in 1776, urged him to consider women's legal position as the new government was shaped. The ideal of republican motherhood gave women a recognized civic role and encouraged the education of girls, but it did not give women the vote or equal legal rights.
Republican motherhood expanded women's civic importance without giving women political rights. It placed women's political role within the home.

records.title: The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
records.heading: The global impact of the Revolution
records.text:
The global impact of the Revolution
The Revolution's ideals helped inspire later independence movements in France, Haiti, and Latin America.
The American Revolution and the ideals set forth in the Declaration of Independence reverberated in France, Haiti, and Latin America, inspiring future independence movements. In France, the American example and ideas about natural rights and popular government helped inspire revolutionaries in 1789. In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, an uprising by enslaved people that began in 1791 led to the independent Republic of Haiti in 1804. In the early 1800s, independence movements spread across Spanish and Portuguese America.
Each of these movements had its own causes and its own leaders, so the American Revolution is best seen as one important influence among several.

State constitutions gave the most power to legislatures, limited governors, and protected rights.

records.title: The Articles of Confederation
records.heading: The Articles of Confederation
records.text:
The Articles of Confederation
The Articles preserved state power and won the war, but a government without the power to tax or regulate trade could not solve postwar problems.
The Articles of Confederation unified the newly independent states, creating a central government with limited power. Congress was the only branch of the national government. Each state had one vote, there was no president, and the national government had no power to tax or to regulate trade among the states. Important laws required the approval of nine of the thirteen states, and changing the Articles required the agreement of all thirteen. The Articles were adopted by Congress in 1777 and went into force in 1781 after all the states had ratified them.
The new government won the war and negotiated the Treaty of Paris of 1783. After the Revolution, however, difficulties over international trade, finances, interstate commerce, foreign relations, and internal unrest led to calls for a stronger central government. Congress had to ask the states for money and could not make them pay. States set up trade barriers against one another, Britain refused to leave forts in the Northwest, and Spain closed the Mississippi River to American navigation in 1784, hurting western settlers.
In 1786–1787, Shays' Rebellion, in which indebted farmers in western Massachusetts shut down courts to stop foreclosures, frightened many leaders. The national government had no army to put down the rebellion and the state had to raise a militia on its own. To many Americans, the episode showed the need for a government able to keep order.

records.title: The Articles of Confederation
records.heading: Settling the West
records.text:
Settling the West
The Northwest Ordinance created a lasting model for admitting new states and banned slavery in the Northwest Territory.
As settlers moved westward during the 1780s, Congress enacted the Northwest Ordinance for admitting new states. The Land Ordinance of 1785 set up a system for surveying and selling western land in orderly townships and set aside land for public schools. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 provided for governing the territory north of the Ohio River and a path to statehood on equal terms with the original states once a territory reached a certain population. The ordinance promoted public education, the protection of private property, and a ban on slavery in the Northwest Territory.
These laws were among the most lasting achievements of the Confederation Congress, and they created a model for how the nation would expand. They did not recognize the land claims of the Native peoples who lived in the region, which led to conflict.

records.title: The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification
records.heading: The Convention and its compromises
records.text:
The Convention and its compromises
Compromises over representation and slavery made the Constitution possible, and the compromises over slavery gave the institution protection.
In the summer of 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia, with Rhode Island absent, and through negotiation, collaboration, and compromise proposed a constitution. They had been called to revise the Articles of Confederation, but they wrote a new plan of government. George Washington presided, and James Madison's notes are the most complete record of the debates.
The delegates first disagreed over representation. The Virginia Plan, supported by large states, called for a strong national government with representation based on population. The New Jersey Plan, supported by small states, called for a single house of Congress with equal representation for each state. The Great Compromise created a House of Representatives based on population and a Senate with two members from each state.
The delegates also compromised over the representation of slave states in Congress and the role of the federal government in regulating both slavery and the slave trade. Under the Three-Fifths Compromise, three-fifths of the enslaved population would be counted for representation and direct taxes. The Constitution allowed the prohibition of the international slave trade after 1808, and it required the return of people who escaped slavery. Delegates from the Deep South made clear that they would not join the new government without such protections, and the compromises gave slavery a protected place in the new government.

records.title: The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification
records.heading: Federalists and Anti-Federalists
records.text:
Federalists and Anti-Federalists
Federalists argued that a large republic with divided power would protect liberty, while Anti-Federalists feared distant, powerful government.
When the Constitution was sent to the states for ratification, Anti-Federalists opposing ratification battled with Federalists, whose principles were articulated in the Federalist Papers, primarily written by Alexander Hamilton and James Madison, with John Jay. Federalists argued that a stronger national government was needed to govern a large country and that the new system would protect liberty by dividing power. In Federalist No. 10, Madison argued that a large republic would make it harder for a single faction to control the government, because there would be many competing interests.
Anti-Federalists, among them Patrick Henry and George Mason, feared that a distant national government would threaten the rights of individuals and the powers of the states. Many believed that republics worked best in small communities where representatives stayed close to the people. They also objected that the Constitution had no bill of rights.
Nine states had to approve the Constitution for it to take effect. Delaware ratified first, in December 1787, and New Hampshire became the ninth state in June 1788. The large states of Virginia and New York ratified after bitter debates.

records.title: The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification
records.heading: The Bill of Rights
records.text:
The Bill of Rights
The promise of a Bill of Rights secured ratification, and the first ten amendments limited the powers of the federal government.
Federalists ensured the ratification of the Constitution by promising the addition of a Bill of Rights that enumerated individual rights and explicitly restricted the powers of the federal government. Several states ratified with recommended amendments. In 1789 the First Congress, led by James Madison, proposed amendments, and ten of them were ratified in 1791. They protected freedom of religion, speech, press, and assembly, the right to bear arms, rights of the accused such as trial by jury, and reserved to the states and the people the powers not given to the federal government.
The Bill of Rights answered a central Anti-Federalist objection and made the new government more acceptable to those who feared central power.
The Bill of Rights was not part of the Constitution as signed in 1787. It was added after ratification, as the price of winning support.

records.text:
The Constitution
How the Constitution created a limited but dynamic national government through federalism and the separation of powers, and what it kept and changed from the Articles and from colonial government.
The Constitution created a limited but dynamic central government that embodied federalism and provided for a separation of powers among three branches.
The CED asks you to explain continuities and changes in the structure and functions of government with ratification of the Constitution. For each feature, ask what it kept from earlier governments and what it changed.

records.title: The Constitution
records.heading: Federalism
records.text:
Federalism
Federalism shares power between the national and state governments and gives the national government specific powers, including taxation and the regulation of commerce.
Delegates from the states participated in the Constitutional Convention that created a limited but dynamic central government embodying federalism. Federalism divides power between the national government and the states. The Constitution gave Congress specific powers, which are called enumerated powers. Article I, Section 8 included the power to lay and collect taxes, to borrow money, and to regulate commerce with foreign nations, among the states, and with the Indian tribes. It also gave Congress the power to make all laws “necessary and proper” to carry out those powers, a clause that allowed the national government to grow in later years.
The Constitution declared itself the supreme law of the land, which meant that valid federal law overrode conflicting state law. Powers not given to the national government remained with the states or the people, a principle later stated in the Tenth Amendment. States kept responsibility for much of daily life, including most criminal law, education, and local government.

records.title: The Constitution
records.heading: Separation of powers and checks and balances
records.text:
Separation of powers and checks and balances
Three branches with checks on one another limit the power of each, and indirect election limited the influence of popular majorities.
The Constitution provided for a separation of powers among three branches. Congress, which makes laws, is divided into a House of Representatives and a Senate. The president, who carries out the laws, is chosen by an Electoral College, and the federal courts interpret the law. Each branch can check the others. The president can veto bills, Congress can override a veto and can impeach officials, the Senate approves treaties and appointments, including federal judges, and the courts decide cases under the Constitution and federal law.
These arrangements reflected the fear of concentrated power that Revolutionary leaders had learned from republican thinkers and from Montesquieu. They also limited excessive popular influence. Senators were chosen by state legislatures and presidents were chosen by electors rather than by direct vote, so only the House was elected directly by voters.
The process of amending the Constitution was made difficult but not impossible, which allowed it to change over time.

records.title: The Constitution
records.heading: Continuities and changes from the Articles
records.text:
Continuities and changes from the Articles
The Constitution kept the republic and the states but gave the national government the structure and powers that the Articles had lacked.
The Constitution kept the republican form of government, the written framework, the states, and a Congress, and it kept many familiar features of colonial and state government, such as elected legislatures with two houses and a division of powers. The Constitution changed the structure of the national government. It created an executive and a national court system, gave the national government direct power to tax and to regulate commerce among the states, provided that federal law was supreme over state law, and replaced one vote per state with representation in the House based on population.
Ratification therefore preserved the republican ideals of the Revolution while correcting the weaknesses that the Articles had shown. Its supporters considered it a stronger government that nonetheless remained limited by law.
The Constitution did not abolish state governments. It created a stronger national government on top of state governments that kept real power.

records.title: Shaping a New Republic
records.text:
Shaping a New Republic
How Washington and Adams put the Constitution into practice, why disputes over economics and foreign policy produced the first political parties, and how the new nation dealt with Britain, Spain, France, and American Indian nations.
In the 1790s the new government built lasting institutions, and disagreements over the nation's economy, foreign policy, and the meaning of the Constitution gave rise to political parties.
The CED asks you to explain how competition intensified conflicts among peoples and nations and how political ideas, institutions, and party systems developed. Keep the domestic and the foreign sides together, because the French Revolution drove both.

records.title: Shaping a New Republic
records.heading: Washington, Adams, and institutions
records.text:
Washington, Adams, and institutions
Washington and Adams made the Constitution work by creating departments, courts, a financial system, and precedents.
During the presidential administrations of George Washington and John Adams, political leaders created institutions and precedents that put the principles of the Constitution into practice. Washington took office in 1789. He appointed department heads, including Alexander Hamilton as Secretary of the Treasury and Thomas Jefferson as Secretary of State, who met with him as a cabinet. The Judiciary Act of 1789 established the federal court system.
Hamilton proposed a financial program to strengthen the national government and its credit. It called for the federal government to pay the national debt and to assume the states' war debts, to create a national bank, and to raise revenue through tariffs and an excise tax on whiskey. His supporters saw a program that would build the nation's economy, while opponents saw a program that favored merchants and speculators and expanded federal power. In 1794 farmers in western Pennsylvania resisted the whiskey tax in the Whiskey Rebellion, and Washington led a large militia force to the region, which demonstrated that the federal government could enforce its laws.
Washington's Farewell Address, published in 1796, encouraged national unity, as he cautioned against political factions and warned about the danger of permanent foreign alliances. Washington decided not to seek a third term, setting a precedent that lasted more than a century.

records.title: Shaping a New Republic
records.heading: Parties and foreign policy
records.text:
Parties and foreign policy
Disputes over the national government's power, the economy, and the French Revolution divided leaders into the first two political parties.
Political leaders in the 1790s took a variety of positions on issues such as the relationship between the national government and the states, economic policy, foreign policy, and the balance between liberty and order. This led to the formation of political parties, most significantly the Federalists, led by Alexander Hamilton, and the Democratic-Republican Party, led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. Federalists favored a strong national government, commerce and manufacturing, and friendly ties with Britain. Democratic-Republicans favored limited national government, a strict reading of the Constitution, agriculture, and sympathy for France.
War between France and Britain resulting from the French Revolution presented challenges to the United States over issues of free trade and foreign policy and fostered political disagreement. Washington issued a Neutrality Proclamation in 1793, but Britain seized American ships and sailors. Jay's Treaty of 1794 settled some disputes and led Britain to remove troops from forts in the Northwest, but it was unpopular with Democratic-Republicans, who thought it favored Britain. Under Pinckney's Treaty of 1795, Spain recognized American rights to navigate the Mississippi River and to store goods at New Orleans, and settled the southern boundary.
Under President Adams, relations with France worsened. In the XYZ Affair, French agents demanded bribes from American diplomats, and an undeclared naval conflict called the Quasi-War followed. The Federalist Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798, which lengthened the residency required for citizenship, allowed the president to deport noncitizens judged dangerous, and made it a crime to publish false or malicious statements against the government. Democratic-Republicans saw the laws as attacks on their party and on freedom of speech. Jefferson and Madison replied with the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, which argued that states could judge the constitutionality of federal laws.
Washington warned against political parties, yet the parties formed during his own presidency. Do not treat the Farewell Address as describing a world without parties.

records.title: Shaping a New Republic
records.heading: Borders, American Indians, and Spanish California
records.text:
Borders, American Indians, and Spanish California
The United States used treaties and force to secure its borders and the Ohio country, while Spain expanded missions in California.
The U.S. government forged diplomatic initiatives aimed at dealing with the continued British and Spanish presence in North America, as U.S. settlers migrated beyond the Appalachians and sought free navigation of the Mississippi River. Pinckney's Treaty addressed the Mississippi question, and Jay's Treaty addressed the British forts.
An ambiguous relationship between the federal government and American Indian tribes contributed to problems regarding treaties and American Indian legal claims relating to the seizure of their lands. The Constitution gave Congress authority over commerce with the tribes, and the government made treaties with them, but states, settlers, and speculators often ignored those agreements. After a Native confederacy in the Ohio country defeated U.S. armies in the early 1790s, General Anthony Wayne defeated it at Fallen Timbers in 1794, and in the Treaty of Greenville of 1795 the tribes gave up much of present-day Ohio.
In the West, the Spanish, supported by the bonded labor of the local American Indians, expanded their mission settlements into California. These missions provided opportunities for social mobility for soldiers and led to new cultural blending, even as Native people suffered from disease and forced labor.

records.title: Developing an American Identity
records.text:
Developing an American Identity
How Americans expressed a national identity after the Revolution in language, literature, art, and architecture, while regional differences continued.
Americans began to create a national culture that expressed republican ideals, but regional differences continued.
The CED asks you to explain the continuities and changes in American culture from 1754 to 1800. This topic is a development topic, so aim to describe a change and explain why it happened.

records.title: Developing an American Identity
records.heading: A new national culture
records.text:
A new national culture
After independence, Americans promoted a distinct national culture through language, education, symbols, and religious freedom.
New forms of national culture developed in the United States alongside continued regional variations. After independence, writers, artists, and educators saw a need to establish a distinctive American culture to match the new republic. Noah Webster's spelling book and later dictionary promoted a standard American usage of English, and school texts taught republican virtue and love of country. Americans celebrated Washington as a national hero, and the symbols of the new nation, including the eagle and the flag, spread.
Many people believed that republican government required an educated citizenry, so there was new attention to schools and to the education of both boys and girls. Americans also dropped many traditional ties to Britain. Several states ended official support for churches, and Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom (1786) separated church and state.

records.title: Developing an American Identity
records.heading: Art, literature, and architecture
records.text:
Art, literature, and architecture
Painters, writers, and architects used American subjects and classical models to express national identity.
Ideas about national identity increasingly found expression in works of art, literature, and architecture. Painters such as Charles Willson Peale and Gilbert Stuart made portraits of Revolutionary leaders, and John Trumbull painted scenes from the Revolution. Writers such as Royall Tyler, whose play The Contrast (1787) contrasted American simplicity with European manners, and Philip Freneau, whose poetry celebrated the Revolution, tried to create a literature with American themes. Phillis Wheatley, an enslaved woman who published poetry in the 1770s, showed that Black writers also took part in this culture.
In architecture, Americans favored a neoclassical style drawing on Greek and Roman models, which they associated with republican government. Thomas Jefferson's design for the Virginia state capitol and his own home, Monticello, are examples, and the new capital city of Washington, D.C., was planned with large public buildings in this style.

records.title: Developing an American Identity
records.heading: Regional variations
records.text:
Regional variations
National identity grew while regional differences in economy, society, and politics continued.
A national culture did not erase regional differences. New England had towns centered on churches and commerce, the Middle Atlantic region had a diverse population and active trade, the South depended on plantation agriculture and slavery, and the backcountry had its own frontier culture. These regions differed over economic, political, social, and foreign policy issues, as the disputes between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans showed.
National identity and regional identity developed side by side, and the tension between them would shape American politics in the decades that followed.

records.title: Movement in the Early Republic
records.text:
Movement in the Early Republic
How American Indian nations adjusted their alliances, how westward migration spread frontier cultures and tensions, and how slavery expanded in the Deep South while antislavery sentiment grew in the North.
Movement of people into the interior intensified competition for land, and the growth of slavery in one region and its decline in another created lasting regional differences.
The CED asks you to explain how migration and immigration caused competition and conflict, and how regional attitudes about slavery changed. This topic builds connections across regions, so practice linking a cause to a pattern.

records.title: Movement in the Early Republic
records.heading: American Indian alliances
records.text:
American Indian alliances
Native nations made shifting alliances to protect their lands, and British support for them added to tensions with the United States.
Various American Indian groups repeatedly evaluated and adjusted their alliances with Europeans, other tribes, and the United States, seeking to limit migration of white settlers and maintain control of tribal lands and natural resources. During the Revolution, Native nations had to choose sides or try to stay neutral, and the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy split, with some nations supporting the Patriots and others the British. The Treaty of Paris of 1783 gave the United States land claimed by Native nations, who were not parties to it.
After the war, a confederation of Native peoples in the Ohio country resisted U.S. expansion with British support. British alliances with American Indians contributed to tensions between the United States and Britain, because British forts remained in the Northwest. These tensions eased after Fallen Timbers in 1794, when Native forces were defeated, and after Jay's Treaty, in which Britain agreed to leave the forts.

records.title: Movement in the Early Republic
records.heading: Westward migration and frontier cultures
records.text:
Westward migration and frontier cultures
Settlers who moved west brought frontier cultures with them and competed for land with Native peoples and one another.
As increasing numbers of migrants from North America and other parts of the world continued to move westward, frontier cultures that had emerged in the colonial period continued to grow, fueling social, political, and ethnic tensions. After the Revolution, settlers crossed the Appalachians into Kentucky and Tennessee, which became states in 1792 and 1796, and into the Ohio country. Many of them were of Scots-Irish and German descent, and they made their living from farming, hunting, and trade.
Frontier settlers wanted secure land titles, protection from Native peoples, and access to markets, especially through the Mississippi River. They often resented eastern elites and federal policies such as taxes, which was the background of the Whiskey Rebellion. Competition for land also meant conflict with Native nations, with the Spanish and British, and among settlers themselves.

records.title: Movement in the Early Republic
records.heading: Slavery and regional attitudes
records.text:
Slavery and regional attitudes
Slavery declined in the North and expanded in the Deep South, which created distinct regional attitudes.
The expansion of slavery in the Deep South and adjacent western lands and rising antislavery sentiment began to create distinctive regional attitudes toward slavery. In the North, states abolished slavery or adopted gradual emancipation, and the Northwest Ordinance banned slavery north of the Ohio River. Free Black communities in northern cities formed churches and aid societies, such as the Free African Society, founded in Philadelphia in 1787 by Richard Allen and Absalom Jones.
In the South, the invention of the cotton gin in 1793 made short-staple cotton profitable and encouraged the spread of slavery into the Deep South and westward. Many white Southerners who had once called slavery an evil came to defend it as necessary. The Constitution protected slavery with the Three-Fifths Compromise, the fugitive slave clause, and the delay of any ban on the international slave trade until 1808. Fear of slave rebellion, heightened by the Haitian Revolution, led Southern states to tighten control of enslaved people.
Slavery was not limited to the South in 1790, and antislavery action was not limited to the North. The pattern was uneven, and it was moving in different directions in different regions.

records.title: Continuity and Change in Period 3
records.text:
Continuity and Change in Period 3
A guide to describing and explaining what stayed the same and what changed in American politics, society, and ideas between 1754 and 1800.
Independence changed who governed and how, but many social patterns, including slavery and inequality, continued.
The CED treats continuity and change as a historical reasoning process. The strongest answers say what stayed the same, what changed, and why, using a specific example for each claim.

records.title: Continuity and Change in Period 3
records.heading: How to reason about continuity and change
records.text:
How to reason about continuity and change
Compare a category at the beginning and the end of the period, and explain the causes of change and the reasons for continuity.
Continuity and change over time means describing what remained the same and what shifted across a period, and explaining why. Start by choosing a starting point and an ending point. For Period 3, those are the colonial situation in 1754 and the new republic in 1800. Then pick a category, such as government, society, or ideas, and describe the state of that category at each end.
A claim about change should name the change, give evidence for it, and explain what caused it. A claim about continuity should name what persisted and explain why it persisted. Strong answers avoid treating a period as all change or all continuity.

records.text: Continuity and change over time means describing what remained the same and what shifted across a period, and explaining why. Start by choosing a starting point and an ending point. For Period 3, those are the colonial situation in 1754 and the new republic in 1800. Then pick a category, such as government, society, or ideas, and describe the state of that category at each end.

records.title: Continuity and Change in Period 3
records.heading: Continuity and change in politics and government
records.text:
Continuity and change in politics and government
Government changed from monarchy to republic, but self-government traditions and debates over central power continued.
The independence movement changed the form of government. Colonists who had been subjects of a monarch built republics, wrote state constitutions and a federal Constitution, and formed political parties. Power moved from Parliament and the Crown to elected American governments, and the Constitution replaced the weak Articles with a stronger national government.
At the same time, much continued. Colonial assemblies became state legislatures, and traditions of local self-government, English legal rights, and fear of concentrated power continued from the colonial period. Property qualifications for voting remained common. Disputes between those who wanted a stronger central government and those who favored local and state power continued from the Articles to the Constitution to the parties of the 1790s.

records.title: Continuity and Change in Period 3
records.heading: Continuity and change in society and ideas
records.text:
Continuity and change in society and ideas
The Revolution changed ideas and some institutions, but slavery, inequality, and Native dispossession continued.
The American independence movement affected society in several ways. Revolutionary ideals led some Americans to challenge slavery, widened women's civic role through republican motherhood, and encouraged a national culture. Northern states ended or began to end slavery, and religious freedom expanded.
Yet slavery continued and grew in the South, women and most free Black men could not vote, and American Indian nations lost land as settlers moved west. The same Revolution that inspired antislavery arguments also left slavery protected in the Constitution. A balanced answer explains both the change and its limits.
Do not say the Revolution changed nothing or everything. Name the specific change, name what stayed the same, and say why.
